title: Guides describe reasoning, not fact lists
statement: A marking guide describes the reasoning that earns credit in a few checks, not facts or keywords, which can be wrong or matched by an answer lacking the reasoning.
example: In one set of short-answer items, wrong facts caused 14 of 18 failures, and a postmortem traced them to the examples the writer put in the guide.
detail: The AP generator's system message tells it that short-answer scoring guidance describes criteria, not evidence lists (`icloud-work/aptraining/.agent/research/inference_clean.md`). In the failure analysis, factual accuracy caused 14 of 18 failures in one course's short-answer items, and a postmortem traced them to the guide itself: the writer filled its sample-response and acceptable-evidence fields with plausible but wrong historical examples (`icloud-work/aptraining/.agent/research/failure_taxonomy.md`). Every fact a guide lists, especially one its writer recalls rather than verifies, is another chance to be wrong.
against: Telling the small writer to leave specific facts out did not work: it wrote wrong specific facts instead (the same analysis). the same note calls that instruction good enough for a large model and insufficient for a 14B one (`icloud-work/ML learnings/sft_v7_benchmark_postmortem.md`). The course's own published guide lists examples: its short-answer scoring guidelines say what credited responses must do and then give "Examples that earn this point include the following:" (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/curriculum/ceds/ap-european-history-ced.pdf`, pdftotext -layout output, line 12660). The same change also removed about 300 lines of other prompt constraints (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/python/benchmark/CHANGELOG_RELENTLESS.md`, line 179), so the drop is not the list change alone. It is design guidance, not a measurement, and for a short recall answer the same library credits any two of an accepted set instead (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0158-assessment-pattern-library-brainlift.qmd`). The fix was not yet tested when the note was written; those runs came before it (same file, line 137). A ban on lists alone did not work: the same report says that for these notes “don’t list specific facts” failed and that verified-facts-only constraints are stronger. The handover's techniques come from a sibling generator whose best run used a different grader version, which it calls design evidence, not certified current scores. In a 15-item replay, short-answer sample responses were too generic for the scorer, and the repair that added concrete examples by topic was one of the changes in the version that passed 15 of 15 (`icloud-work/aptraining-crystal-copy-20260521/full-copy/aptraining-root/parallel-ideas-lab/experiments/failed_export_replay/RUNNING_SUMMARY.md`, lines 205-225); that version repaired an existing run rather than a fresh one (line 249). The same BrainLift keeps full automation for numeric, diagram and property-based answers with explicit tolerances, where the space of valid answers is small.

Students and generators can imitate rubric terms without performing the historical work. A sentence beginning "Although" is not automatically complex. Mentioning purpose is not sourcing. Naming two events is not comparison. The course scores the relationship between claim, evidence, and historical object, not the presence of a phrase.
Meaning scoring replaced substring detection everywhere (a word detector wearing a rubric's clothes praises listed words in wrong sentences).
The displayed praise and “That holds up” response do not establish that a student’s interpretation is true or well supported.
"He wanted to be Othellos ancient but Cassio got to be the ancient" has the ranks backwards, but it met "someone else got it".
The open word response is stored for review rather than judged correct by a keyword match.
The course scores the relationship between claim, evidence, and historical object, not the presence of a phrase.
The largest risks are a guide that sounds like a younger product in disguise, and a judge that grades evidence by keyword when Grade 9 asks for reasoning.
| The judge rewards matching quotes, not reasoning | Rubric criteria for relevant and sufficient evidence and for reasoning that links them (RI.9-10.8) |
**RI.9-10.8:** "Delineate and evaluate the argument… whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning."
The LLM rubric should grade how relevant and sufficient the evidence is, and the reasoning, not just whether a matching span was found.
